claim: Axon fasciculation plays a key role in the development of neural networks.
source: While axon fasciculation plays a key role in the development of neural networks, very little is known about its dynamics and the underlying biophysical mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: Very little is known about the dynamics and underlying biophysical mechanisms of axon fasciculation.
source: While axon fasciculation plays a key role in the development of neural networks, very little is known about its dynamics and the underlying biophysical mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Axons dynamically interact with each other through their shafts, leading to zippering and unzippering behavior that regulates their fasciculation.
source: we observed that axons dynamically interact with each other through their shafts, leading to zippering and unzippering behavior that regulates their fasciculation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Zippering arises from the competition of axon-axon adhesion and mechanical tension in the axons.
source: We show that zippering arises from the competition of axon-axon adhesion and mechanical tension in the axons
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by biophysical analysis and modeling.

claim: This study provides the first quantification of the force of axon-axon adhesion.
source: and provide the first quantification of the force of axon-axon adhesion.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution in the abstract and supported by BFP measurements.

claim: Mechanical tension regulates axon fasciculation through the control of axon shaft zippering.
source: Our study uncovers a new role of mechanical tension in neural development: the regulation of axon fasciculation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by experimental manipulations and modeling.

claim: Complex neural networks are built through the growth of axons from their neuronal cell body of origin toward their target(s), according to specific pathfinding patterns (Chédotal and Richards, 2010).
source: In the developing nervous system, complex neural networks are built through the growth of axons from their neuronal cell body of origin toward their target(s), according to specific pathfinding patterns (Chédotal and Richards, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Axon pathfinding patterns are genetically controlled by molecular cues mediating interactions between axons and their environment, including other axons, cells and the extracellular matrix (Kolodkin and Tessier-Lavigne, 2011).
source: These patterns are genetically controlled by molecular cues mediating interactions between axons and their environment, including other axons, cells and the extracellular matrix (Kolodkin and Tessier-Lavigne, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The establishment of axonal projections is in many cases a multistep process, in which individual axons are sequentially guided from one area to another by a series of cues inducing specific decisions at the level of axonal growth cones (Mann et al., 2004).
source: The establishment of axonal projections from a given neural tissue to its final target is in many cases a multistep process, in which individual axons are sequentially guided from one area to another by a series of cues inducing specific decisions at the level of axonal growth cones (Mann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A fundamental principle governing axon pathfinding resides in the control of the fasciculation and defasciculation of their axons.
source: a fundamental principle governing axon pathfinding resides in the control of the fasciculation and defasciculation of their axons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Control of fasciculation/defasciculation is believed to be exerted at the level of axonal growth cones, which may choose to grow along other axons (fasciculation) or to detach from other axons (defasciculation) (reviewed in [Honig et al., 1998]).
source: This control is believed to be exerted at the level of axonal growth cones, which may choose to grow along other axons (fasciculation) or to detach from other axons (defasciculation) (reviewed in [Honig et al., 1998]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Fasciculation ensures robust coordinated growth of a number of axons along the paths initially established by pioneering axons (Raper and Mason, 2010).
source: On the one hand, fasciculation ensures robust coordinated growth of a number of axons along the paths initially established by pioneering axons (Raper and Mason, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Axon defasciculation, often associated to branching, is in many cases required for individual axons to reach with precision their specific target(s), which can be distributed in large areas (Tang et al., 1994; Schneider and Granato, 2003).
source: On the other hand, axon defasciculation, often associated to branching, is in many cases required for individual axons to reach with precision their specific target(s), which can be distributed in large areas (Tang et al., 1994; Schneider and Granato, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Motor axons emerging from spinal somatic motoneurons fasciculate in tight bundles, migrate in fascicles within spinal nerves, and thereafter defasciculate to allow each individual axon subpopulation to innervate a specific muscle cell group (Bonanomi and Pfaff, 2010; Huettl et al., 2012).
source: For example, motor axons emerging from spinal somatic motoneurons fasciculate in tight bundles, they migrate in fascicles within spinal nerves, and they thereafter defasciculate to allow each individual axon subpopulation to innervate a specific muscle cell group (Bonanomi and Pfaff, 2010; Huettl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The interaction of growth cones with other axons has been the focus of numerous studies (Honig et al., 1998; Tang et al., 1994; Lin and Forscher, 1993; Van Vactor, 1998; Kalil, 1996).
source: While the interaction of growth cones with other axons has been the focus of numerous studies (Honig et al., 1998; Tang et al., 1994; Lin and Forscher, 1993; Van Vactor, 1998; Kalil, 1996)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Other aspects of the process of axon fasciculation have received much less attention.
source: other aspects of the process of axon fasciculation have received much less attention.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Very little is known about the dynamics of shaft-shaft interactions, the underlying biophysical mechanisms, and their potential role in the regulation of axon fasciculation.
source: In particular, while it seems obvious that tight fasciculation of axons is aided by adhesion between their shafts, very little is known about the dynamics of shaft-shaft interactions, the underlying biophysical mechanisms, and their potential role in the regulation of axon fasciculation.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The mouse olfactory epithelium comprises a single population of neurons, the olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs).
source: This system has the advantage of comprising a single population of neurons, the olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the model system.

claim: During their normal development from the olfactory epithelium (OE) toward their target in the olfactory bulb (OB), OSN axons undergo a massive fasciculation step to form branches of the olfactory nerve, followed by their defasciculation and rearrangement in the OB to project to their specific target cells distributed throughout the OB glomerular layer (Key et al., 2002; Nedelec et al., 2005; Strotmann and Breer, 2006; Mombaerts, 2006; Mori and Sakano, 2011).
source: During their normal development from the olfactory epithelium (OE) toward their target in the olfactory bulb (OB), OSN axons undergo a massive fasciculation step to form branches of the olfactory nerve, followed by their defasciculation and rearrangement in the OB to project to their specific target cells distributed throughout the OB glomerular layer (Key et al., 2002; Nedelec et al., 2005; Strotmann and Breer, 2006; Mombaerts, 2006; Mori and Sakano, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: It is currently technically challenging to image mouse OSN axon fasciculation and defasciculation dynamics in vivo.
source: Since it is currently technically challenging to image mouse OSN axon fasciculation and defasciculation dynamics in vivo
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation.

claim: It is impossible to manipulate in vivo the individual axons in order to assess their biophysical properties.
source: and impossible to manipulate in vivo the individual axons in order to assess their biophysical properties
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation.

claim: OSN axons interact extensively with each other through their axon shafts, leading to zippering and unzippering behaviors that trigger their fasciculation or defasciculation, respectively.
source: Surprisingly, we observed that OSN axons interact extensively with each other through their axon shafts, leading to zippering and unzippering behaviors that trigger their fasciculation or defasciculation, respectively.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction, supported by experimental observations.

claim: OSN axons grow in cultures as unbranched axons.
source: OSN axons grow in cultures as unbranched axons.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: The growth of OSN axons from OE explants was characterized by a sequence of three main stages: (1) advance of the growth cones and initiation of an axon network (first 24–48 hr), (2) maintenance of the growth cones at distance from the explants, but with little or no further growth (48–72 hr), and (3) retraction of the growth cones and collapse of the network (3–5 d).
source: In our experimental conditions (see Materials and methods), the growth of these axons from OE explants was characterized by a sequence of three main stages: (1) advance of the growth cones and initiation of an axon network (first 24–48 hr), (2) maintenance of the growth cones at distance from the explants, but with little or no further growth (48–72 hr), and (3) retraction of the growth cones and collapse of the network (3–5 d).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: The initial axon network, composed of individual axons or bundles of few axons, progressively evolves into a less dense network with thicker bundles.
source: During this stage, the initial axon network, composed of individual axons or bundles of few axons, progressively evolves into a less dense network with thicker bundles
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse recordings and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The total length of the network and the total number of vertices (junction points) decreased approximately linearly with time in the interval examined.
source: Based on this image analysis, we determined the total length of the network and the total number of vertices (junction points), and found that both these quantities decreased approximately linearly with time in the interval examined (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from image analysis, shown in Figure 1H.

claim: This trend was observed in five out of six quantitatively analyzed experiments from different cultures, with an average reduction of (20 ± 16)% in length of the network over the duration of the recordings (178 to 295 min).
source: This trend was observed in five out of six quantitatively analyzed experiments from different cultures, with an average reduction of (20 ± 16)% in length of the network over the duration of the recordings (178 to 295 min).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from multiple experiments.

claim: The dynamics of the axon network is topologically reminiscent of the well-known coarsening of two-dimensional foams (Glazier and Weaire, 1992; Weaire and Hutzler, 2001).
source: Topologically, such dynamics is reminiscent of the well-known coarsening of two-dimensional foams (Glazier and Weaire, 1992; Weaire and Hutzler, 2001)
evidence: This is an analogy drawn to previous work on foams.

claim: The underlying structures and forces in the axon network are substantially different from those in two-dimensional foams.
source: the underlying structures and forces, however, are substantially different (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated as a distinction from the foam analogy.

claim: In an advancing zippering process, two axons or axon fascicles progressively adhere to each other in a longer segment of contact and form a larger fascicle.
source: In an advancing zippering process, two axons or axon fascicles progressively adhere to each other in a longer segment of contact and form a larger fascicle.
evidence: This is observed in the time-lapse recordings and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Receding zippers leading to defasciculation of axons were also observed.
source: Receding zippers leading to defasciculation of axons were also observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: The zipper vertex at the meeting point of the axons moves with a velocity of the order of 1 μm/min until it reaches a position of equilibrium.
source: The zipper vertex at the meeting point of the axons moves with a velocity of the order of 1μmmin until it reaches a position of equilibrium (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Numerous and frequent zippers were observed throughout the network.
source: Numerous and frequent zippers were observed throughout the network, as demonstrated in Figure 3
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Numerous network vertices displayed structures in which individual or small bundles of axons are adherent to each other along a defined segment, while remaining parallel to each other.
source: We observed at high magnification that numerous network vertices displayed structures as shown in Figure 4B,C, in which individual or small bundles of axons are adherent to each other along a defined segment, while remaining parallel to each other.
evidence: This is observed in SEM images shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: A zipper with laminar structure is free to increase or decrease the length of the zippered segment, depending on the balance of the forces acting at the zipper vertex; such zippers are called 'simple zippers'.
source: A zipper with such structure is free to increase or decrease the length of the zippered segment, depending on the balance of the forces acting at the zipper vertex; we call such zippers 'simple zippers'.
evidence: This is a definition based on the observed structure.

claim: Zippers with entangled structure were observed more rarely.
source: More rarely, we observed zippers with entangled structure (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is an observation from SEM images shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Entangled structure may prevent the zipper from unzippering past the entanglement point; further zippering, however, remains possible.
source: Such structure may prevent the zipper from unzippering past the entanglement point; further zippering, however, remains possible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structure.

claim: In some instances, axons would cross on top of each other, without forming a zippered segment.
source: In some instances, axons would cross on top of each other, without forming a zippered segment (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from SEM images shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Thin lateral protrusions emerging from the shafts are observed in the network.
source: Besides axon shafts and their bundles, thin lateral protrusions emerging from the shafts are observed in the network (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is an observation from SEM images shown in Figure 4G.

claim: These protrusions appear highly dynamic and occasionally mediate interactions at a distance when they extend and touch another axon shaft.
source: These protrusions appear highly dynamic and occasionally mediate interactions at a distance when they extend and touch another axon shaft.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: The progressive coarsening of the axon network results from zippering events driven by adhesion between the axon shafts.
source: The observations reported above indicate that the progressive coarsening of the axon network results from zippering events driven by adhesion between the axon shafts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations.

claim: In recorded time lapse sequences of network evolution in 13 explants, the axon network typically coarsened or appeared stable.
source: In recorded time lapse sequences of network evolution in 13 explants, we typically observed that the axon network coarsened in a manner similar to Figure 1, or in some cases appeared stable when the recording was performed over shorter time intervals.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from multiple experiments.

claim: Zippering events dominated over unzippering events in general.
source: This indicates that, in general, zippering events dominated over unzippering events.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that networks typically coarsened.

claim: In a few cases, a de-coarsening dynamics was seen in a limited area of the network, associated with an apparent contraction of the explant, thus generating a pulling force on the axonal network.
source: In a few cases, however, a de-coarsening dynamics was seen in a limited area of the network. Upon examining these cases, we noticed that they were associated with an apparent contraction of the explant, thus generating a pulling force on the axonal network (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The application of 5% FBS reliably induced the explant pull.
source: Interestingly, while no obvious effect on the growth cones was observed upon FBS addition to the culture, we found that the application of 5% FBS reliably induced the explant pull.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: The FBS-induced pull is likely due to a cell-rounding effect of FBS on cultured neurons, previously demonstrated in Jalink and Moolenaar (1992).
source: This is likely due to a cell-rounding effect of FBS on cultured neurons, previously demonstrated in Jalink and Moolenaar (1992).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: FBS addition resulted in de-coarsening in the axon network in some cases.
source: In Figure 5A–D, an example is shown, with a resulting de-coarsening in the axon network.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: Often, the FBS-induced pull resulted in a rapid collapse of the entire axon network onto the explant, due presumably to a disturbance of the attachments of the axons to the substrate.
source: Often, however, the FBS-induced pull resulted instead in a rapid collapse of the entire axon network onto the explant, due presumably to a disturbance of the attachments of the axons to the substrate.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: 10 μM blebbistatin did not show visible effect on axon tension, but rather had a stabilizing effect on the network: the spontaneous coarsening was inhibited while the individual zippers remained mobile.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, in our culture system 10 μM blebbistatin (dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)) did not show visible effect on axon tension, but rather had a stabilizing effect on the network: the spontaneous coarsening was inhibited while the individual zippers remained mobile.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: No stabilizing effect was observed in control experiments in which only DMSO was added.
source: No such effect was observed in control experiments in which only DMSO was added.
evidence: This is an observation from control experiments.

claim: FBS applied to the pre-stabilized network rapidly induced clear de-coarsening in parts of the network, with unzippering/defasciculation dominating over zippering events.
source: In Figure 5E–H and I–L, two examples are shown in which FBS was applied to the pre-stabilized network and rapidly induced clear de-coarsening in parts of the network, with unzippering /defasciculation dominating over zippering events.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 5E–H and I–L.

claim: The edge of the explant retreated by approximately 20 μm, thus stretching the axon network in the horizontal direction.
source: In the example of Figure 5E–H, the edge of the explant (visible near the left border of each frame) retreated by approximately 20 μm to the left, thus stretching the axon network in the horizontal direction.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 5E–H.

claim: The lengths of the paths increased by (8–23) μm, that is by 4–10%, during the first 20 min after FBS was added.
source: The lengths of the paths increased by (8–23) μm, that is by 4–10% (panel E in Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from image analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The paths tended to become more straight during the first 20 min after FBS was added.
source: while at the same time, the paths tended to become more straight (panel F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from image analysis, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The axon segments became significantly stretched and also aligned in the direction of the pull, as expected for an object under increased tension.
source: The axon segments thus became significantly stretched and also aligned in the direction of the pull, as expected for an object under increased tension.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed stretching and alignment.

claim: The stretching of the axons by ∼15 μm is expected to result in a significant tension increase of over 1 nN.
source: The stretching of the axons by ∼15 μm is expected to result in a significant tension increase of over 1 nN (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on expected axon stiffness.

claim: This tension increase is achieved within 20 min of FBS addition and precedes the changes in network configuration.
source: This tension increase is achieved within 20 min of FBS addition and precedes the changes in network configuration seen in Figure 5G–H.
evidence: This is an inference from the timing of observations.

claim: 2 μM cytochalasin B induces a change in network dynamics consistent with a drop of average axon tension.
source: Indeed we found that in our system, 2 μM cytochalasin B (dissolved in DMSO) induces a change in network dynamics consistent with a drop of average axon tension.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: The application of cytochalasin B induced coarsening in a network that was previously stable.
source: In the example in Figure 6A–C, the application of cytochalasin B induced coarsening (panel C) in a network that was previously stable (panels A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: Cytochalasin B induces strong network coarsening within 30 min of application in networks that were pre-stabilized by blebbistatin.
source: As shown in the example frames in Figure 6D–F and in the graphs in Figure 6G–I, cytochalasin B induces strong network coarsening within 30 min of application.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 6D–F and Figure 6G–I.

claim: No coarsening effect was observed in control experiments in which only DMSO was applied.
source: No such effect was observed in control experiments in which only DMSO was applied.
evidence: This is an observation from control experiments.

claim: The zipper will be in static equilibrium when the effective tensile forces are in balance with the force of adhesion between the axons.
source: The zipper will be in static equilibrium when the effective tensile forces are in balance with the force of adhesion between the axons.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement from the biophysical model.

claim: For a symmetric zipper, the force balance condition in the direction parallel to the zippered segment is given by S=2T(1−cos⁡β2).
source: At the vertex of the zipper (Figure 7A), the force balance condition in the direction parallel to the zippered segment is given by(1)S=2T(1−cos⁡β2)
evidence: This is a theoretical equation derived from the biophysical model.

claim: The typical value of mechanical tension in an isolated axon grown in culture is of the order of 1 nN.
source: It is known from previous literature that the typical value of mechanical tension in an isolated axon grown in culture is of the order of 1 nN ([Dennerll et al., 1988] reports a wide range of rest tension values, with the most common tension around 0.5 nN).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The small diameter of OSN axons (about 200 nm) makes the use of calibrated needles or MEMS difficult for tension measurement.
source: In our case, the small diameter of OSN axons (about 200 nm) makes the use of such approaches difficult, because of the likely physical contact of the manipulator with the substrate resulting in an incorrect force reading, as well as in the detachment of the axon from the substrate.
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation.

claim: Optical tweezers technique does not permit to achieve manipulation forces comparable to 1 nN.
source: Optical tweezers technique would in principle allow the manipulation using microbeads attached to axons without touching the substrate, but does not permit to achieve manipulation forces comparable to 1 nN.
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation.

claim: The BFP technique uses a red blood cell as a force transducer.
source: In this technique, streptavidin-coated glass microbeads (3 μm diameter) attached to biotinylated axons are manipulated by a biotinylated red blood cell aspirated in a micropipette (Evans et al., 1995; Gourier et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the BFP technique, supported by citations.

claim: By measuring the deformation of the red blood cell, one can calculate the force with which the bead is manipulated.
source: By measuring the deformation of the red blood cell, one can calculate the force with which the bead is manipulated.
evidence: This is a description of the BFP technique.

claim: The distribution of axon tensions is sharply peaked near 678 pN, with the mean value of 679 pN and the interquartile range (529–833) pN.
source: The distribution is sharply peaked near 678 pN, with the mean value of 679 pN and the interquartile range (529–833) pN.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from BFP measurements, shown in Figure 8F.

claim: An increase in tension from (432 ± 157) pN to (1665 ± 219) pN was observed in one axon, likely caused by strong stretching of the axon.
source: For one of the axons, two distinct values of tension were measured early and late in the experiment: (432 ± 157) pN and (1665 ± 219) pN. This increase in tension was likely caused by the strong stretching of the axon that occurred during this particular experiment—see Figure 8—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from BFP measurements, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of equilibrium zipper angles is sharply peaked around 42°, with mean of 51.2° and interquartile range (34–60)°.
source: The distribution is sharply peaked around 42°, with mean of 51.2° and interquartile range (34–60)°.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from zipper angle measurements, shown in Figure 7C.

claim: By dragging one of the axons of a zipper, the zipper angle was increased beyond its equilibrium value, leading to unzippering accompanied by a decrease of angle.
source: By dragging one of the axons of a zipper, we increased the zipper angle beyond its equilibrium value, leading to unzippering accompanied by a decrease of angle (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: This is an observation from micromanipulation experiments, shown in Figure 9A–D.

claim: After the axon was released by lifting the pipette, the axons snapped back to a smaller zipper angle which initiated a re-zippering process accompanied by an increase of the angle, leading finally to the recovery of the initial configuration.
source: Then, the axon was released by lifting the pipette. The axons snapped back to a smaller zipper angle which initiated a re-zippering process accompanied by an increase of the angle (Figure 9E–F), leading finally to the recovery of the initial configuration.
evidence: This is an observation from micromanipulation experiments, shown in Figure 9E–F.

claim: In both advancing and receding zippers, the zipper vertex moves with a velocity in the range (0.3−2) μm/min.
source: It can be seen that in both advancing (Figure 10A) and receding (Figure 10B) zippers, the zipper vertex moves with a velocity in the range (0.3−2)μmmin.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from tracking individual zippers, shown in Figure 10A,B.

claim: Some zippers converge with an approximately constant velocity, while others have a weakly exponential velocity profile, with the velocity gradually decreasing as equilibrium is approached.
source: Figure 10C shows that while some zippers (R3 and A6) converge with an approximately constant velocity, others (R4 and A5) have a weakly exponential velocity profile, with the velocity gradually decreasing as equilibrium is approached.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from tracking individual zippers, shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The case in which the zipper stops rather abruptly near the equilibrium position is observed in roughly 2/3 of the evaluated examples.
source: The former case, in which the zipper stops rather abruptly near the equilibrium position, is observed in roughly 2/3 of the evaluated examples.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from tracking individual zippers.

claim: The angle increases with time for advancing zippers and decreases with time for receding zippers.
source: In Figure 10D, the smoothed zipper angle is plotted as a function of time for three advancing and two receding zippers. In these examples, the angle increases with time for advancing zippers (A1, A4, A6) and decreases with time for receding zippers (R4, R5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from tracking individual zippers, shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Different forms of dominating friction lead to distinct paths as well as time courses of the trajectory.
source: It is seen that different forms of dominating friction (black for viscous elongation, red for substrate friction, blue for vertex-localized friction) lead to distinct paths (Figure 12A) as well as time courses (Figure 12B,D) of the trajectory.
evidence: This is a prediction from the biophysical model, shown in Figure 12A,B,D.

claim: A typical response of a zipper to a fast asymmetric perturbation consists of a fast lateral equilibration, followed by a slower dynamics during which the vertex moves parallely to the zippered segment.
source: Our experimental observations (as in Figure 9) show that a typical response of a zipper to a fast asymmetric perturbation consists of a fast lateral equilibration, followed by a slower dynamics during which the vertex moves parallely to the zippered segment.
evidence: This is an observation from micromanipulation experiments, shown in Figure 9.

claim: Such trajectory arises from the model in case of dominant zipper friction, while it cannot be achieved through the other friction mechanisms alone.
source: Such trajectory arises from our model in case of dominant zipper friction (blue line), while it cannot be achieved through the other friction mechanisms alone.
evidence: This is a prediction from the biophysical model.

claim: The velocity of zippering is primarily limited by the internal friction localized at the zipper vertex.
source: We conclude that the velocity of zippering is primarily limited by the internal friction localized at the zipper vertex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: An approximately constant velocity of zippering is obtained in the model when the tension is assumed to increase gradually over an extended interval of minutes, rather than abruptly.
source: An approximately constant velocity of zippering is obtained in the model, however, when the tension is assumed to increase gradually over an extended interval of minutes, rather then abruptly (Figure 12E).
evidence: This is a prediction from the biophysical model, shown in Figure 12E.

claim: In the developing network, the zippering is driven by gradual, rather than abrupt, changes in the forces that act at the zipper vertex.
source: These results suggest that in the developing network, the zippering is driven by gradual, rather than abrupt, changes in the forces that act at the zipper vertex.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: The comparison of predictions of the dynamical model with experimental observations supports a framework in which the zippering arises from an imbalance of tension and adhesion forces at the zipper vertex, and in which the zippering velocity is limited predominantly by friction arising from internal energy dissipation in the immediate vicinity of the moving vertex.
source: To summarize, the comparison of predictions of the dynamical model with experimental observations supports a framework in which the zippering arises from an imbalance of tension and adhesion forces at the zipper vertex, and in which the zippering velocity is limited predominantly by friction arising from internal energy dissipation in the immediate vicinity of the moving vertex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing model predictions with experimental observations.

claim: The gradual decrease of the total network length with time indicates that zippering is overall more frequent than unzippering.
source: The gradual decrease of the total network length with time (Figure 1H) indicates that in our experimental setting, zippering is overall more frequent than unzippering.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The observed decrease of the total number of vertices is a natural consequence of zippering.
source: The observed decrease of the total number of vertices (Figure 1H) is likewise a natural consequence of zippering.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation shown in Figure 1H.

claim: A process repeatedly observed in the developing network consisted of a gradual collapse of triangular loops, with the three vertices eventually converging into a single-vertex quasi-stable configuration.
source: A process of this type repeatedly observed in the developing network (Figure 3G–J) consisted of a gradual collapse of triangular loops, with the three vertices eventually converging into a single-vertex quasi-stable configuration.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 3G–J.

claim: During the collapse of triangular loops, the loops typically retained their shape, that is the three zipper angles remained approximately constant during the collapse.
source: During this process, the loops typically retained their shape, that is the three zipper angles remained approximately constant during the collapse.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: Such dynamics is expected to result from a decrease in the tension of the axons that constitute the loop, such that the equilibrium zipper angle becomes larger than the current zipper angles.
source: Such dynamics is expected to result from a decrease in the tension of the axons that constitute the loop, such that the equilibrium zipper angle becomes larger than the current zipper angles.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed dynamics.

claim: FBS-induced pulling leads to the rapid opening and expansion of triangular loops in the de-coarsening areas of the network.
source: A strong support for this interpretation of the mechanism of loop collapse is provided by the experiments in which we used FBS to generate a pull on the network, hence increasing axon tension. As seen in Figure 5F–H, this manipulation leads to the rapid opening and expansion of triangular loops in the de-coarsening areas of the network.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 5F–H.

claim: The time scale for a simple zippering or unzippering process is of order 10–20 min.
source: As the time scale for a simple zippering or unzippering process is of order 10–20 min (see Results)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental observations.

claim: The coarsening of the network develops over hours.
source: while the coarsening of the network develops over hours.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: Such separation of time scales indicates that the network is locally near the quasi-equilibrium state corresponding to the momentaneous values of the axon tensions.
source: Such separation of time scales indicates that the network is locally near the quasi-equilibrium state corresponding to the momentaneous values of the axon tensions.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed time scales.

claim: At a given time, the majority of vertices in the network are approximately static or fluctuating around an equilibrium position, while the proportion of steadily advancing or receding zippers is minor.
source: At a given time, the majority of vertices in the network are seen to be approximately static or fluctuating around an equilibrium position, while the proportion of steadily advancing or receding zippers is minor (see Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Video 1.

claim: The majority of the zippers have a zipper angle that is close to the equilibrium value given by Equation 1.
source: In the following analysis, we will assume that the majority of the zippers have a zipper angle that is close to the equilibrium value given by Equation 1 (see also Discussion).
evidence: This is an assumption based on the observed network dynamics.

claim: The median angle of the distribution shifted to lower values during the 3 hr interval (from 60° to 49°).
source: In the example of Figure 14A (which corresponds to Figure 1D-H), the median angle of the distribution shifted to lower values during the 3 hr interval (from 60° to 49°).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from image analysis, shown in Figure 14A.

claim: The distribution of the fasciculation incidence angles in Roberts and Taylor (1982) is similar to the distribution of zipper angles measured in our system.
source: As shown in the inset of Figure 15, the distribution of the fasciculation incidence angles in (Roberts and Taylor, 1982) is similar to the distribution of zipper angles measured in our system.
evidence: This is a comparison shown in Figure 15.

claim: Small angles (between 0° and 30°) are notably absent from the recorded angle distributions.
source: Small angles (between 0° and 30°) are notably absent from the recorded angle distributions (see also Figure 14A)
evidence: This is an observation from the angle distributions shown in Figure 14A and Figure 15.

claim: Roberts and Taylor proposed that the under-representation of small angles was a result of zippering processes analogous to the ones that we directly observed in our study.
source: Roberts and Taylor proposed that this was a result of zippering processes analogous to the ones that we directly observed in our study.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Roberts and Taylor (1982).

claim: If a growing axon encounters another axon at an initially small incidence angle and starts following it, the segment behind the growth cone subsequently zippers and the incidence angle increases until the equilibrium zipper angle is reached.
source: Thus, if a growing axon encounters another axon at an initially small incidence angle and starts following it (Figure 13B1,B2), the segment behind the growth cone subsequently zippers and the incidence angle increases until the equilibrium zipper angle is reached (Figure 13B3).
evidence: This is an inference supported by the observations and shown in Figure 13B1,B2,B3.

claim: The under-representation of small angles in the zipper angle distributions supports the inference that most zippers are close to local equilibrium during the development of the network.
source: The under-representation of small angles in the zipper angle distributions (Figures 14A and 15) thus further supports our inference that most zippers are close to local equilibrium during the development of the network.
evidence: This is an inference supported by the observations shown in Figures 14A and 15.

claim: A good agreement with the crossing probabilities reported in Roberts and Taylor (1982) is seen.
source: A good agreement with the crossing probabilities reported in Roberts and Taylor (1982) is seen.
evidence: This is a comparison shown in Figure 15.

claim: The framework successfully applied to explain the network properties observed in the in vivo study of Roberts and Taylor (1982) is not limited to dynamics in culture.
source: We thus successfully applied our framework to explain the network properties observed in the in vivo study of Roberts and Taylor (1982), indicating that this framework is not limited to dynamics in culture.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison with Roberts and Taylor (1982).

claim: Axon fasciculation is generally thought to be controlled during development at the level of growth cones, which may adhere to other axons in their environment (hence driving fasciculation), or may separate from other axons (hence driving defasciculation).
source: Axon fasciculation is generally thought to be controlled during development at the level of growth cones, which may adhere to other axons in their environment (hence driving fasciculation), or may separate from other axons (hence driving defasciculation).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: This study provides strong evidence for an additional mechanism playing a critical role in regulating axon fasciculation, which does not involve growth cones, but takes place at the level of axon shafts, through zippering of individual axons or small bundles of axons.
source: Here, we provide strong evidence for an additional mechanism playing a critical role in regulating axon fasciculation, which does not involve growth cones, but takes place at the level of axon shafts, through zippering of individual axons or small bundles of axons.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: In the culture of embryonic olfactory epithelium explants, the zippering mechanism resulted in a substantial reorganization of the structure of a grown axon network, on the time scale of 10 hr.
source: In our culture of embryonic olfactory epithelium explants, this mechanism resulted in a substantial reorganization of the structure of a grown axon network, on the time scale of 10 hr.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The process of axon zippering has been rarely reported or discussed in previous literature.
source: The process of axon zippering has been rarely reported or discussed in previous literature.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Axon zippering in vivo was inferred in Roberts and Taylor (1982) and was noticed for axons growing in culture in Voyiadjis et al. (2011) and Barry et al. (2010).
source: Axon zippering in vivo was inferred in Roberts and Taylor (1982) and was noticed for axons growing in culture in Voyiadjis et al. (2011) and Barry et al. (2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The process of zippering and the underlying biophysical mechanisms were never studied before this work.
source: The process of zippering and the underlying biophysical mechanisms, however, were never studied.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Using a combination of experimental observations and biophysical modeling, axon zippering was shown to arise from the competition of two principal forces: axon-axon adhesion and mechanical tension.
source: Using a combination of experimental observations and biophysical modeling, we showed that axon zippering arises from the competition of two principal forces: axon-axon adhesion and mechanical tension.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The adhesion force favors an increase in the length of the zippered segment.
source: The adhesion force favors an increase in the length of the zippered segment.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement from the biophysical model.

claim: The mechanical tension tends to minimize the total length of the axons, thus favoring unzippering.
source: The mechanical tension tends to minimize the total length of the axons, thus favoring unzippering.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement from the biophysical model.

claim: The relative strength of adhesion and tension forces determines the vertex angle between axons in a zipper that reached static equilibrium.
source: The relative strength of these two forces determines the vertex angle between axons in a zipper that reached static equilibrium.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement from the biophysical model.

claim: The BFP technique was used to measure the mechanical tensions of the OSN axons grown ex vivo, obtaining values (interquartile range (529–833) pN) comparable to tensions reported in the previous literature for PC-12 neurites grown in culture, on average around 650 pN (Dennerll et al., 1988).
source: We used the BFP technique to measure the mechanical tensions of the OSN axons grown ex vivo, and obtained values (interquartile range (529–833) pN) comparable to tensions reported in the previous literature for PC-12 neurites grown in culture, on average around 650 pN (Dennerll et al., 1988).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by BFP measurements and comparison with previous work.

claim: This is the first experimental estimate of the force of adhesion between axon shafts, in any system.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first experimental estimate of the force of adhesion between axon shafts, in any system.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: Selected zippers were unzipped by manipulating them with micropipettes, with consequent re-zippering after the manipulation was stopped.
source: We were able to unzip selected zippers by manipulating them with micropipettes, with consequent re-zippering after the manipulation was stopped.
evidence: This is an observation from micromanipulation experiments.

claim: By fitting induced zippering/unzippering dynamics to a basic biophysical model, an independent estimate of the axon-axon adhesion force was obtained, comparable with the estimate based on static observations.
source: By fitting such induced zippering/unzippering dynamics to a basic biophysical model, we obtained an independent estimate of the axon-axon adhesion force, comparable with the estimate based on static observations.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of micromanipulation experiments.

claim: The results provide a first systematic characterization of the statics and dynamics of individual axon zippers.
source: Our results provide a first systematic characterization of the statics and dynamics of individual axon zippers.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The dynamical biophysical model that was developed makes it possible to include axon zippering in mathematical models of axon guidance and bundling.
source: The dynamical biophysical model that we developed (see Materials and methods) makes it possible to include axon zippering in mathematical models of axon guidance and bundling.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the study.

claim: Previous modeling studies focused on the dynamics of the growth cone, and modeled growth cone guidance by diffusible guidance cues (Goodhill and Urbach, 1999), the influence of tension forces and anchor points/focal adhesions on growth cone trajectory (Li et al., 1995; Nguyen et al., 2016), as well as contact interactions of growth cones with other axons (Hentschel et al., 1999; Chaudhuri et al., 2011).
source: Such studies previously focused on the dynamics of the growth cone, and modeled growth cone guidance by diffusible guidance cues (Goodhill and Urbach, 1999), the influence of tension forces and anchor points/focal adhesions on growth cone trajectory (Li et al., 1995; Nguyen et al., 2016), as well as contact interactions of growth cones with other axons (Hentschel et al., 1999; Chaudhuri et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The previous modeling studies did not consider the dynamics of axon shafts.
source: The previous modeling studies did not, however, consider the dynamics of axon shafts.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The tendency to fasciculate was often interpreted as arising from differential adhesion, that is, the growth cone having stronger adhesion to another axon than to the substrate (Acheson et al., 1991; Roberts and Taylor, 1982).
source: In the previous literature, the tendency to fasciculate was often interpreted as arising from differential adhesion, that is, the growth cone having stronger adhesion to another axon than to the substrate (Acheson et al., 1991; Roberts and Taylor, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The structure of the small fascicles observed in this system, with axons travelling on top of each other, does indicate that adhesion between axon shafts is stronger than axon-substrate adhesion.
source: The structure of the small fascicles observed in our system, with axons travelling on top of each other (Figure 4), does indicate that adhesion between axon shafts is stronger than axon-substrate adhesion.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed structure shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the zippering of axon shafts to occur, differential advantage is in principle not necessary.
source: We note, however, that for the zippering of axon shafts to occur, such differential advantage is in principle not necessary.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement.

claim: Two axon shafts (or axon fascicles) adhered to the substrate can gain mutual adhesion energy by initiating zippering, while remaining adhered to the substrate.
source: Two axon shafts (or axon fascicles) adhered to the substrate can gain mutual adhesion energy by initiating zippering, while remaining adhered to the substrate (as in the configurations shown in Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by the observed configurations shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: In the biophysical analysis, it was assumed that adhesion to the substrate was preserved during zippering.
source: In our biophysical analysis, we assumed that adhesion to the substrate was preserved during zippering
evidence: This is stated as an assumption of the biophysical model.

claim: The possible subsequent slower rearrangements (involving loss of substrate contact for some axons) in the internal structure of the zippered fascicle were not modeled.
source: and we did not model the possible subsequent slower rearrangements (involving loss of substrate contact for some axons) in the internal structure of the zippered fascicle.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the biophysical model.

claim: A striking observation is that the axon network, initially established as a complex network of individual axons or small bundles of axons, progressively coarsens in time, leading to the formation of large fascicles of axons.
source: A striking observation, in our culture system, is that the axon network, initially established as a complex network of individual axons or small bundles of axons, progressively coarsens in time, leading to the formation of large fascicles of axons.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the experimental system.

claim: The coarsening persists over time scales of about 10 hr, which is much longer than the typical time scale for an individual zippering process (10 min).
source: The coarsening persists over time scales of about 10 hr, which is much longer than the typical time scale for an individual zippering process (10 min).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental system.

claim: It is unlikely that the coarsening is a result of protracted equilibration of zipper configurations under stationary force conditions.
source: It is therefore unlikely that the coarsening is a result of protracted equilibration of zipper configurations under stationary force conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed time scales.

claim: A possible explanation of the slow coarsening dynamics may lie in a gradual decrease of the average axon tension as the culture matures, which would lead to increasing domination of axon-axon adhesion forces over tension, hence favoring zippering.
source: A possible explanation of the slow coarsening dynamics may lie in a gradual decrease of the average axon tension as the culture matures, which would lead to increasing domination of axon-axon adhesion forces over tension, hence favoring zippering.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation.

claim: This proposal is supported by the observed sequence of stages of the culture maturation: axon elongation in the early stage, insignificant elongation in the intermediate stage and axon retraction in the final stage.
source: This proposal is supported by the observed sequence of stages of the culture maturation: axon elongation in the early stage, insignificant elongation in the intermediate stage and axon retraction in the final stage.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system that supports the proposed explanation.

claim: According to Dennerll et al. (1989), axonal elongation is possible only when the axon tension exceeds a certain threshold (estimated as 1 nN for PC-12 axons).
source: According to Dennerll et al. (1989), axonal elongation is possible only when the axon tension exceeds a certain threshold (estimated as 1 nN for PC-12 axons)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In this system, the arrest of growth in the intermediate stage may have resulted from a decrease of tension below the threshold for elongation.
source: in our system, the arrest of growth in the intermediate stage may thus have resulted from a decrease of tension below such threshold.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on previous work.

claim: Further indications of decreased tension are observed near the end of the intermediate stage, when some growth cones visibly loose their grip to the substrate, and hence can no longer generate axon tension by pulling (Lamoureux et al., 1989).
source: Further indications of decreased tension are observed near the end of the intermediate stage, when some growth cones visibly loose their grip to the substrate (see Video 4), and hence can no longer generate axon tension by pulling (Lamoureux et al., 1989).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Video 4, and supported by a citation.

claim: When cytochalasin was applied to a slowly coarsening or stabilized network, a marked increase in coarsening rate resulted within 30 min of the application.
source: Indeed, we found that when the drug was applied to a slowly coarsening or stabilized network, a marked increase in coarsening rate resulted within 30 min of the application (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Apart from the more pronounced coarsening, cytochalasin did not change the structure of the network, and the axons did not become visibly slack.
source: Apart from the more pronounced coarsening, cytochalasin did not change the structure of the network, and the axons did not become visibly slack
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: This is consistent with the expected reduction of tension in all directions in the evolving network, with enough tension remaining to keep the axons taut.
source: this is consistent with the expected reduction of tension in all directions in the evolving network, with enough tension remaining to keep the axons taut.
evidence: This is an inference from the observations.

claim: Morphological changes (the growth cone acquiring a stub-like shape with suppressed filopodia, and a reduction in number of axonal side processes) were observed, consistent with previous studies (Dennerll et al., 1988; Letourneau et al., 1987) in which cytochalasin-induced reduction of axon tension was assessed.
source: While we did not measure the axon tension in cytochalasin-treated cultures, we did observed morphological changes (the growth cone acquiring a stub-like shape with suppressed filopodia, and a reduction in number of axonal side processes) consistent with previous studies (Dennerll et al., 1988; Letourneau et al., 1987) in which cytochalasin-induced reduction of axon tension was assessed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, consistent with previous work.

claim: In cytochalasin-treated cultures, the axons took a longer time (16 min in two experiments, compared to 6 and 10 min for untreated network) to detach from the substrate and retract when exposed to trypsin, presumably because longer proteolysis of adhesion molecules is needed before the reduced tension can detach the axons (Letourneau et al., 1987).
source: Similarly to (Letourneau et al., 1987), we also observed that in cytochalasin-treated cultures, the axons took a longer time (16 min in two experiments, compared to 6 and 10 min for untreated network) to detach from the substrate and retract when exposed to trypsin, presumably because longer proteolysis of adhesion molecules is needed before the reduced tension can detach the axons (Letourneau et al., 1987).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, consistent with previous work.

claim: Blebbistatin is an inhibitor of NMII, previously shown to decrease cell cortex/membrane tension in non-neuronal cells (Fischer-Friedrich et al., 2014; Ayala et al., 2017) and to decrease tension generated in smooth muscle (Ratz and Speich, 2010).
source: As a second strategy aiming to perturb axon tension, we tested blebbistatin, an inhibitor of NMII, previously shown to decrease cell cortex/membrane tension in non-neuronal cells (Fischer-Friedrich et al., 2014; Ayala et al., 2017) and to decrease tension generated in smooth muscle (Ratz and Speich, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In growth cones of isolated DRG neurons, Sayyad et al. (Sayyad et al., 2015) showed that blebbistatin reduced the force exerted by lamellipodia, but surprisingly increased the force exerted by filopodia.
source: In growth cones of isolated DRG neurons, Sayyad et al. (Sayyad et al., 2015) showed that blebbistatin reduced the force exerted by lamellipodia, but surprisingly increased the force exerted by filopodia.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Other studies found that the blebbistatin-dependent NMII inhibition may have opposite effects on axon extension, depending on the substrate.
source: Other studies found that the blebbistatin-dependent NMII inhibition may have opposite effects on axon extension, depending on the substrate.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies.

claim: In Ketschek et al. (2007), while inhibition of NMII promoted peripheral dorsal root ganglia (DRG) axon extension on polylysine, it decreased axon extension on laminin.
source: For example, in Ketschek et al. (2007), while inhibition of NMII promoted peripheral dorsal root ganglia (DRG) axon extension on polylysine, it decreased axon extension on laminin.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Hur et al. (Hur et al., 2011), who observed a positive effect of blebbistatin on DRG axon extension on a laminin substrate (thus the opposite result), discussed how these puzzling differences may be due to differences in laminin concentrations, or to the different adhesive properties of polylysine and polyornithine.
source: Hur et al. (Hur et al., 2011), who observed a positive effect of blebbistatin on DRG axon extension on a laminin substrate (thus the opposite result), discussed how these puzzling differences may be due to differences in laminin concentrations, or to the different adhesive properties of polylysine (used in [Hur et al., 2011] and in our study) and polyornithine (used by [Ketschek et al., 2007]).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: These studies suggest that while blebbistatin decreases cell cortex contractility, its effect on axon shaft tension may depend on additional factors.
source: These studies suggest that while blebbistatin decreases cell cortex contractility, its effect on axon shaft tension may depend on additional factors.
evidence: This is an inference from previous studies.

claim: In this model system, no obvious effect of blebbistatin on axon tension or on axon extension was observed.
source: In our model system, we did not observe an obvious effect of blebbistatin on axon tension or on axon extension.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: Further analyses would be required to explain why blebbistatin has a stabilizing effect on OSN axons grown in the experimental conditions.
source: Further analyses would be required to explain why blebbistatin has a stabilizing effect on OSN axons grown in our experimental conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction.

claim: Since the biological agents having the ability to specifically stimulate axon growth or motility in the cultured explants are currently unknown, FBS was tested for this purpose, because of its established content of a variety of bioactive molecules and growth factors.
source: Since the biological agents having the ability to specifically stimulate axon growth or motility in our cultured explants are currently unknown, we tested FBS for this purpose, because of its established content of a variety of bioactive molecules and growth factors.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental approach.

claim: FBS did not have any significant boosting effect on OSN growth cones but induced the apparent contraction of the whole explant itself, leading to the generation of pulling forces on axons from the explant core.
source: It turned out that FBS did not have any significant boosting effect on OSN growth cones but, very interestingly, it induced the apparent contraction of the whole explant itself, leading to the generation of pulling forces on axons from the explant core.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system.

claim: This apparent contraction of the explant is likely to be the result of changes in the shape of the individual cells constituting the explant, if such changes lead to an overall rounding of previously flattened or elongated cells.
source: This apparent contraction of the explant is likely to be the result of changes in the shape of the individual cells constituting the explant, if such changes lead to an overall rounding of previously flattened or elongated cells.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation.

claim: A quantitative estimate of the increase in axon tension due to the FBS-induced pull may be obtained from the measured stretch of the axons and the expected axon elongation stiffness.
source: A quantitative estimate of the increase in axon tension due to the FBS-induced pull may be obtained from the measured stretch of the axons and the expected axon elongation stiffness.
evidence: This is stated as a method for estimating tension increase.

claim: This is further supported by tension measurements in the experiment of Figure 8—figure supplement 1, where a pull of 6 μm was correlated with increase of tension by about 1.2 nN.
source: This is further supported by our tension measurements in the experiment of Figure 8—figure supplement 1, where a pull of 6 μm was correlated with increase of tension by about 1.2 nN.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from BFP measurements, shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The estimated FBS-induced tension increase of at least 1 nN (possibly several nN) is very significant compared to the typical axon tension (under 1 nN) that was recorded in the untreated networks.
source: The estimated FBS-induced tension increase of at least 1 nN (possibly several nN) is very significant compared to the typical axon tension (under 1 nN) that we recorded in the untreated networks.
evidence: This is a comparison of the estimated tension increase with the measured baseline tension.

claim: This tension increase, which was achieved within 20 min of the application of FBS, preceded a marked and rapid de-coarsening in parts of the network.
source: This tension increase, which was achieved within 20 min of the application of FBS, preceded a marked and rapid de-coarsening in parts of the network (Figure 5F-H).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental system, shown in Figure 5F-H.

claim: On the network level, it was shown that the extent of axon fasciculation can be regulated by changes in axon tension: an overall decrease in tension leads to zippering-driven coarsening, while an overall increase in tension leads to unzippering and de-coarsening.
source: We have thus shown on the network level that the extent of axon fasciculation can be regulated by changes in axon tension: an overall decrease in tension leads to zippering-driven coarsening, while an overall increase in tension leads to unzippering and de-coarsening.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: The estimated tension increase (of order 1 nN) generated endogenously by the FBS-induced explant pull is comparable in magnitude to active changes in axon tension demonstrated in previous literature, such as the tension recovery within 30 min after axon unloading in vitro (Dennerll et al., 1989) and in vivo (Rajagopalan et al., 2010).
source: The estimated tension increase (of order 1 nN) generated endogenously by the FBS-induced explant pull is comparable in magnitude to active changes in axon tension demonstrated in previous literature, such as the tension recovery within 30 min after axon unloading in vitro (Dennerll et al., 1989) and in vivo (Rajagopalan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work, supported by citations.

claim: The results demonstrate the control of axon zippering by tension changes of functionally relevant magnitude.
source: Our results therefore demonstrate the control of axon zippering by tension changes of functionally relevant magnitude.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.
